newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan bank pledge stands but safety net may shrink.
newsitem.headline: Japan bank pledge stands but safety net may shrink.

text.p: Japan is sticking by its pledge not to let major banks fail, but as troubled institutions cut back their operations and give up their overseas ambitions they may find they are no longer part of the government safety net.

Japanese officials made their "too big to fail" statement two years ago to ease fears fanned in foreign markets of a financial meltdown after the nation suffered its first bank failure of the postwar era.
But as big banks pull out of overseas operations and become less significant global entities, they may find the government less willing to rush to their rescue.

"What they are saying is that they don't want Japanese banks to cause trouble in world markets, that they are worried about the impact in New York and London (of a Japanese bank failure)," said one banking analyst.

Troubled Nippon Credit Bank Ltd announced on Tuesday that it would halt overseas operations as part of a major restructuring that also includes selling off its Tokyo headquarters and posting losses to dispose of problem loans.

Separately, Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, Japan's 10th biggest commercial bank, and regional rival Hokkaido Bank Ltd announced they would merge next April, and Takushoku would withdraw from overseas operations by next March.

Many Japanese banks have already scaled back their overseas presence, which in the heady days of the late 1980s raised fears of Japanese dominance as the institutions expanded business by making loans with razor-thin margins.

More are likely follow suit given the unprofitability of much of their overseas business and pressure to slough off the burden of problem loans still on the books some seven years after the collapse of Japan's asset price "bubble."

"It's already happening. The great late '80s hubris has by and large disappeared," said David Threadgold, financial analyst at BZW Securities. "They are taking a more sensible approach to what they are doing and why."

Some analysts said ultimately about five Japanese banks would maintain a serious presences in European and America -- perhaps Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd, Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd, Sumitomo Bank Ltd, Sanwa Bank Ltd and Fuji Bank Ltd.
"The rest of the city banks are probably going to have a tough time making it outside of Asia," the analyst said.

The August 1995 collapse of Hyogo Bank Ltd was accompanied by the shutdown of the nation's biggest credit union and quickly followed by news that Daiwa Bank Ltd had suffered huge losses on unauthorised bond deals by a New York trader.

Last November, authorities for the first time decided to liquidate a troubled regional bank, Hanwa Bank Ltd, rather than deal with its collapse by setting up a new institution as happened with Hyogo and another small regional bank.

Authorities say Hanwa was a different story from Nippon Credit Bank because of Hanwa's small scale and domestic focus. "Our top priority is to prevent the problems of Japanese banks from causing trouble for foreign creditors," Sei Nakai, a deputy direcor-general at the Finance Ministry's Banking Bureau, said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television.
Asked whether all Japanese banks which now have presences overseas would continue to do so, Nakai said: "I think this is something that the market will decide."

He added: "It depends on each bank's ability and market competition, but as financial authorities, we will keep close watch so that when they withdraw (from overseas), there is no trouble for foreign creditors."
